title: You never committed it — but you did stage it once
summary: reset --hard destroyed an hour of uncommitted work. There is no reflog entry for it. But if you ran git add even once, the content is in the object database — go and get it.
mental_model: `git add` does not just record a path — it writes the file's content into `.git/objects` as a blob, immediately. Resetting removes the index entry, but nothing deletes that blob. If it was ever staged, it exists.
danger: This only works for content that was staged at some point. A file edited and never added is genuinely gone after reset --hard — no git command can recover it.

steps.title: Look at what is about to be lost
steps.why: analysis.py is staged. scratch.py is not — it has never been through `git add`. That distinction is the entire difference between recoverable and gone.
steps.expect: analysis.py has an index entry with a blob hash. scratch.py is just ??.

steps.title: Destroy everything
steps.why: `reset --hard` matches index and working tree to HEAD; `clean -fd` removes the untracked leftovers. This is the standard 'start from scratch' pair, fired at the wrong moment.
steps.expect: Both files gone from disk. Nothing in the reflog refers to them — they were never commits.

verify.label: both files are gone from the working tree

steps.title: Confirm the usual routes are dead ends
steps.why: The reflog only records commits. There is no commit here, so there is nothing for it to show. This is the point at which most people conclude the work is gone.
steps.expect: One commit, no stashes, nothing useful.

steps.title: Ask for dangling blobs
steps.why: `fsck` reports objects nothing points at — and `git add` wrote analysis.py into the object store as a blob. It is unreferenced now, but it is still sitting there.

verify.label: the staged content is still in the object database

steps.title: Read the blob
steps.why: `cat-file -p` prints any object by hash. Before restoring, confirm it is the file you want — a busy repository can have several dangling blobs from different abandoned operations.
commands: sh -c 'for sha in $(git fsck --lost-found 2>/dev/null | grep "dangling blob" | cut -d" " -f3); do echo "== $sha"; git cat-file -p $sha; done'
steps.expect: Your analysis code, printed straight out of .git/objects.

steps.title: Write it back to disk
steps.why: Redirect the blob's content into a file and it is recovered. There is no metadata — no filename, no timestamp — because a blob is only content. You supply the name.

actions.run: sh -c 'git cat-file -p $(git fsck --lost-found 2>/dev/null | grep "dangling blob" | cut -d" " -f3 | head -1) > analysis.py'

verify.label: the staged file was recovered from a dangling blob

steps.title: Commit it before anything else happens
steps.why: It is recovered but still uncommitted, which is exactly the state that lost it in the first place. Commit now; admire it later.
steps.expect: Two commits. scratch.py is still gone, and always will be — it was never staged.

verify.label: the never-staged file is genuinely unrecoverable
the staged-then-destroyed file was recovered and committed
verify.hint: git fsck --lost-found, then git cat-file -p <blob> > analysis.py

verify.label: the file that was never staged is gone for good — no command recovers it

pitfalls: This only works because `git add` writes a blob immediately. Content that was only ever edited on disk is not in git at all.
A dangling blob has no filename. If several files were staged you must read each one to tell them apart.
`git gc --prune=now` deletes dangling blobs. Do not tidy up before recovering.
The real lesson is upstream: `git stash -u` before any `reset --hard` costs two seconds and makes all of this unnecessary.

write a recovered blob back to disk
the blob hash behind each staged file
